# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is an optimization technique used during autoregressive inference in transformer models. During each generation step, the model processes all previous tokens to predict the next token. Without caching, this would require recomputing the key and value projections for every token in the context at every step—a quadratic cost that makes long sequences computationally prohibitive.

The KV cache stores the computed key and value matrices from previous tokens in memory, so they need only be computed once. At each new step, the model computes keys and values only for the newly added token, then appends them to the existing cache. This reduces the per-token computation from O(n) to O(1), transforming the overall complexity from O(n²) to O(n).

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Long-context models face a fundamental tension: extending context length increases memory usage and computational costs. KV cache directly addresses this by making longer contexts tractable. Without it, generating text with a context of 128K tokens would require recomputing attention over millions of token pairs. With KV cache, the model processes each new token in constant time relative to context length.

However, KV cache introduces its own scaling challenges. The cache grows linearly with sequence length and must fit in GPU memory. This has driven innovations like grouped-query attention, key-value pooling, and architecture changes such as MQA and GQA that reduce the memory footprint per token. KV cache is an optimization technique used during autoregressive inference in transformer models. The KV cache solves this by storing the key and value matrices from previously processed tokens in memory. When generating a new token, the model only computes the projections for the new token, then retrieves the cached keys and values for the context. This reduces the per-token computation from O(n) to O(1), dramatically improving inference efficiency.

For very long contexts, this memory pressure becomes the primary bottleneck rather than compute. This has driven innovations like grouped-query attention, paged attention, and quantization schemes that reduce the memory footprint while preserving the computational benefits.

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is a memory optimization technique used during autoregressive language model inference that stores and reuses the key and value matrices from previous token computations. When a language model processes a sequence token by token, each token's representation depends on all preceding tokens through the attention mechanism. Without caching, the model would need to recompute the entire attention context from scratch for every new token, repeatedly processing the same tokens already seen. The KV cache eliminates this redundancy by preserving the computed keys and values in memory, allowing the model to attend to the full context without redundant computation.

## How It Works

During each forward pass, the model projects input tokens into query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices. The attention mechanism computes attention scores by taking the dot product of queries with keys, applies softmax to get attention weights, and then multiplies these weights by the values to produce the output. Once keys and values for a token have been computed, they never change—subsequent tokens only add new queries to interact with this existing context. The KV cache stores these frozen key-value pairs, so each new token only needs to compute its own query and then perform attention against the accumulated cache rather than reprocessing everything.

# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## The Computational Bottleneck in Autoregressive Generation

Large language models generate text token by token in an autoregressive manner—each new token depends on all previously generated tokens. In the attention mechanism, computing relationships between tokens requires projecting inputs into query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices. During generation, when producing token N, the model must recompute Q, K, and V projections for tokens 1 through N-1, even though these computations were already performed when generating previous tokens. This redundant work creates a quadratic computational burden that scales with sequence length, making long-context generation prohibitively expensive without optimization.

## How KV Cache Solves This

KV cache addresses this inefficiency by storing computed key and value matrices from previous tokens and reusing them in subsequent forward passes. When generating each new token, the model only computes Q, K, and V for the current token, then performs attention between this new query against the cached keys and values from all prior tokens. This transforms the attention computation from O(N²) per step to O(N), where N is the current sequence length. The cache grows incrementally as generation proceeds, containing the accumulated key-value pairs that represent the model's "memory" of the context.
